title: A bill to deny admission to the United States to any representative to the United Nations who has been found to have been engaged in espionage activities or a terrorist activity against the United States and poses a threat to United States national security interests.
official_summary:
(This measure has not been amended since it was passed by the Senate on April 7, 2014. The summary of that version is repeated here.)

Amends the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Years 1990 and 1991 to direct the President to deny U.S. admission to any representative of the United Nations (U.N.) who: (1) has been found to have been engaged in espionage activities or a terrorist activity against the United States or its allies, and (2) may pose a threat to U.S. national security interests.

summary.headline: This law directs the President to bar United Nations representatives who engaged in spying or terrorism against the U.S. from entering the country.
summary.what_it_does: The law amends an earlier foreign relations statute to tell the President to deny U.S. entry to any United Nations representative who has been found to have engaged in espionage or terrorist activity against the United States or its allies. The representative must also be someone who may pose a threat to U.S. national security. The summary does not describe how such findings are made or what review process applies.

who_it_affects.group: United Nations representatives seeking to enter the United States
who_it_affects.how: Those found to have engaged in espionage or terrorist activity against the U.S. or its allies, and who may pose a national security threat, can be refused admission.
They are directed to deny admission in covered cases, so they must apply this standard when reviewing UN representatives' entry requests.
